claims.quote: Most patients can be diagnosed without testing.

claims.text: MRI (perhaps MRA) as soon as possible for thunderclap headache, altered mental status, meningismus, papilledema or acute focal deficit; CT if MRI is not immediately available.
claims.quote: MRI (and perhaps magnetic resonance angiography [MRA]) should be done as soon as possible in patients with any of the following findings: Thunderclap headache Altered mental status Meningismus Papilledema Acute focal neurologic deficit If MRI is not immediately available, CT can be used.

claims.text: Neuroimaging (usually MRI) also for a subacute deficit, new onset, age > 50, cancer, HIV, a changed headache pattern or diplopia.
claims.quote: Neuroimaging, usually MRI, should also be done if patients have any of the following: Focal neurologic deficit of subacute or uncertain onset New onset Age > 50 years Cancer HIV infection Change in an established headache pattern Diplopia

claims.text: Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis when meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage or encephalitis is considered; thunderclap headache needs CSF analysis even with normal imaging, unless imaging contraindicates LP.
claims.quote: In addition, if meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, encephalitis, or any cause of meningismus is being considered, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis should be done, if not contraindicated by imaging results. Patients with a thunderclap headache require CSF analysis even if imaging and examination findings are normal as long as lumbar puncture is not contraindicated by imaging results.

claims.text: ESR and CRP for visual symptoms, jaw or tongue claudication, temporal artery signs or other signs of giant cell arteritis.
claims.quote: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) should be determined if patients have visual symptoms, jaw or tongue claudication, temporal artery signs, or other findings suggesting giant cell arteritis.

claims.text: Tonometry if findings suggest acute narrow-angle glaucoma.
claims.quote: Tonometry should be done if findings suggest acute narrow-angle glaucoma

claims.text: LP and CSF analysis for progressive headache suggesting idiopathic intracranial hypertension or chronic meningitis.
claims.quote: Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis are done if headache is progressive and findings suggest idiopathic intracranial hypertension (eg, transient obscuration of vision, diplopia, pulsatile intracranial tinnitus) or chronic meningitis
